I currently have a hard time understanding what Tau Ceti contains. Here are some things I think would improve the situation:

  1. A visual summary of the progress of each roadmap. I've had Claude mock up a prototype here. Once I get some feedback, I can make a PR to add this to the Tau Ceti website (as another Progress tab at the top). I'm happy to restyle it to align with the current website.
  2. We need to think about how external agents can search Tau Ceti for results they need. The current grep approach is not the greatest; I had Claude analyze some options and write them up here. If we can come to a consensus about which of these are good ideas I'm happy to help work on some of them.
  3. Longer term, I think it will be helpful to have some kind of view on what mathematics should get added to roadmaps, rather than relying on what people who are involved in Tau Ceti are interested in. Something like doing a census of graduate math textbooks (and perhaps other sources) and looking at what Tau Ceti contains and what it is missing. But there's no urgency here, since it's currently very easy to find interesting math that's not yet in Tau Ceti. :grinning:
My account got suspended by Github (not sure why). The links are broken for now; I'm appealing.

Lean Pool uses Octo search for better search. I would recommend Tau Ceti to adopt it as well. CC
@Austin Letson for more info.

OctoSearch would allow agents to search the most up to date branch through the public MCP.

Setting up OctoSearch is pretty easy if you want to give it a try. Essentially you install a read only GitHub app and then it will automatically create the search index. There are instructions here: https://axiomatic-ai.github.io/octo/setup-search/

I am happy to help with anything!

OctoSearch can also be configured to allow searching the branch the agent is developing. I think it would be interesting to test this capability in the A/B testing for code review. I am happy to collaborate with the Tau Ceti team if this is of interest.
Yes I think this would be interesting to try

Also, we seem to be collecting a good number of roadmaps. I wonder if instead of having them listed alphabetically, we should start putting them into folders by broad area? like geometry, number theory, graph theory...?

I've been recording my worker sessions to build a TauCetiBench to allow for A/B testing. I was planning on testing the effect of local loogle, but I'll look into OctoSearch. I hope to have a demo within a couple of days

My appeal to reinstate my Github account (roed-math) was successful (after 2 weeks). So the earlier links are now functional again:

  • visual summary of progress
  • external agent search.

@Chris Birkbeck thought that the visual summary was worth having, so I'm going to proceed with making a PR for that. Additional feedback is welcome.
Was the suspension related to automated use for Tau Ceti?

Tangentially (I think). I was working to create a worker setup for a new desktop machine I bought for LLM use; I'm not sure exactly what automated limit I hit, but I think that there was a claim mechanism I was testing that triggered GIthub.

For the visual summary, maybe it's better to have more visual clues and stats, but light on text, they are better for human consumption.

This is the design principle behind my visual summary pages for the roadmaps my agents are focusing on, e.g. SpinRepresentations and GeometricTopology.

They highlight dependencies and potential routes in the roadmap, math node completeness, PR activity/health timeline etc, and have hover details and links to PRs. I use them to observe and fix what went wrong in the process (working on wrong roadmap targets, PR quality issues due to model/harness defects).

Not all of these apply to the focus of visual summary of progress. Maybe you can ask your agent to check if anything worth absorbing? They are both self-contained, data-oriented single-page static html that my agent update from time to time after my local preview.

Sure, I'll take a look.

I made four changes based on your summaries:

  1. Links to the layer lines in the readme.
  2. Include open PRs in the status.
  3. Allow coverage markers to save a remaining variable
  4. Links to external roadmaps summaries (like yours).

Thanks!

I'll probably make a PR later today and put a note here; happy to incorporate other feedback in the meantime.
See TauCeti#7502 (the new status page on the Tau Ceti website, live demo here) and TauCetiProgress#14 (the supporting changes to the progress infrastructure). Both need human review!

David Roe said:

  1. Longer term, I think it will be helpful to have some kind of view on what mathematics should get added to roadmaps, rather than relying on what people who are involved in Tau Ceti are interested in. Something like doing a census of graduate math textbooks (and perhaps other sources) and looking at what Tau Ceti contains and what it is missing. But there's no urgency here, since it's currently very easy to find interesting math that's not yet in Tau Ceti. :grinning:

I absolutely agree with this. I think that mathlib made some mistakes here (this is just my opinion and I think other maintainers disagree). At the beginning the principle was "get an undergraduate degree in but remember to make really robust API for each definition", then it was "go for stretch goals and fill in what you need along the way", and now many of the stretch goals are being done downstream and the maintainers' views seem to range from "come up with a list of targets and simply close PRs which don't work towards them" (which is where I'm leaning) to "let anyone contribute anything and let's see what happens organically" and because of maintainer disagreement on this matter it seems impossible to write down a coherent plan for where the repo is going and we revert to the default (which is "see what happens organically").

But I would not aim for textbooks. I think the goals should be much harder and, like mathlib, we should aim for these goals and then fill in what is necessary in a robust way.

Example of a stretch goal: I have 150 informal statements of theorems from recent issues of the Annals and these need around 1000 definitions of which mathlib has none. I think Tau Ceti would be perfect for these. But going back to the topic of this thread, it would be good to have the infrastructure so we can see where we are and where we're going. I guess my point is that I want where we're going to be "these 1000 definitions" or "these 150 theorem statements" and hopefully the answer will scale to this.

I agree that textbooks is not an final goal, though it may be a reasonable way to get an initial list of targets in an easily defined way. Your Annals project aligns well with one of my main goals for Tau Ceti: to provide the foundation so that formalizing new mathematics research doesn't require formalizing a bunch of background.

One thing that I think Sage did well was to create a mission statement that helped answer the question of what is "in scope." For Sage, this was "to create an open-source alternative to Mathematica, Matlab, Maple and Magma." For Tau Ceti, I think we basically already have one (though not stated explicitly as a mission statement). Looking at the main README, I see "To build a reusable and open library of formal mathematics, that others can freely build on top of."

I think there's room for multiple overlapping goals within this framework. Graduate textbooks is one; able to state Annals papers is another. Reusable background needed to formalize my new research paper is another. As long as these efforts are working together in a way to build a reusable library, I think there's room for all of them.

One thing that I struggle with is that for frontier research, it's less clear what reusable means, since your new definitions may have just proven a big open problem, but your paper has only just landed so has no citations so how do you prove it's reusable.

If things keep going as they are, it doesn't seem crazy to me to think that we may be in the situation that AI, say, proves BSD next year. I'd really want to have that in tauceti asap. Sure we could just put it in leanpool but I think the process of adding it tauceti "filters" and helps classify where the work fits in wrt the rest of the library/maths (which I think will become increasingly valuable in this AI explosion we are seeing).

It feels to me that if we "just" aim for the reusable bits of all of maths, then we could be done with this sooner than we expect (i.e. maybe some AI swarm descends on tauceti and just does it all in 88hours). Instead of then having to make a tauceti+ to then contain all of the ongoing research, I would think we could plan for this sooner and allow areas of ongoing research that a roadmap reviewer deems important.
Tl;dr with a name like tauceti we should maybe aim higher than reusable.

See "Progress" in the menu bar at the top of the page.
TauCetiProgress#14 is important for supporting TauCeti#7502 since current progress reports don't have the information necessary to support updating the progress page.

David Roe said:

  • external agent search.

If you want to you can add OctoSearch (#General announcements > Axiomatic Octo Search: Semantic Search for Any Lean Projects) to the semantic search options. You currently can't directly search the TauCeti repo itself, but you can index and search any fork of your own, and make your fork searchable by others if you want.

If someone with TauCeti admin rights also thinks it's interesting, ideally they can enable it for the main repo (it takes about one minute).
